statementFromManual.quote: Each terminal is identified by a letter printed below it, and by the number printed at the top of the section in which it is located.
statementFromManual.citation: Book I, p.4 (USING THE PROGRAMMING WIRES)

sectionTerminals.letterOrdinal: the letter is silkscreened BELOW the hole pair; the section number 1..6 is silkscreened at the top of the section, above the BINARY OUTPUT lamp
sectionTerminals.citation: Book I p.4; panel photograph image_3.jpg (all six sections)

letterSetUsed.evidence: Exhaustive token census over the OCR of all three PDFs (all six books): every shorthand token of the form <digit><letter> that occurs is drawn from exactly the 22 designators above. D is reserved for Decimal Input-Output, M for Matrix; I/O/Q are absent (presumably to avoid confusion with 1 and 0).
letterSetUsed.citation: book1.txt + book2-3-4.txt + book5-6.txt, whole-corpus token census; corroborated by the silkscreen in image_3.jpg

commonTerminals.quote: (The notation for a connection to a common terminal is "1com", "2com," etc.)

matrixTerminals.quote: The matrix terminals are designated by: M = matrix / 6 = terminal number (1 to 11) / t = top or "b" for bottom  . . . for example M6t
matrixTerminals.notes: Cells 1-9 carry the t/b suffix. M10 and M11 are single terminals and are written bare (M10, M11) throughout Books V and VI — no M10t/M10b occurs. Two further terminals in the same block are written M+ and M- (see matrixPowerTerminals).

decimalTerminals.quote: The contacts are designated by: D = Decimal Input-Output / 8 = terminal number (1 to 19) . . . for example D8. The contact on the wiper arm is referred to as "D16."
decimalTerminals.discrepancy: The manual writes '(1 to 19)' but a D0 terminal demonstrably exists: the panel dial is silkscreened 0..15 with a hole pair under position 0 (image_3.jpg), the under-panel drawing on the same page p.20 shows a contact at 0, and D0 is used 13 times in program listings across Books IV, V and VI (e.g. 'D15/D0', '5N/D0', '1J/D0', '5Y/D0'). Treat the real range as D0..D19 (20 terminals).

wiringShorthand.quote: A WIRING SHORTHAND is used to indicate connections which are to be made on the computer by simply writing the two terminal designations with a slash in between. In Experiment 1, terminal 1+ was connected to terminal 1A. This is written in shorthand 1+/1A

generalRule.quote: Each terminal has two holes side-by-side which are connected together underneath the computer panel. Programming wires may be plugged into either (or both) holes of the terminal.

exceptions.quote: The terminals with four holes labeled COMMON may be used when more than two connections must be made to a set of terminals on the computer panel.
exceptions.citation: Book I, p.25; hole count confirmed visually in image_3.jpg (four holes inside one printed oval per section)

exceptions.evidence: image_3.jpg crop: each is drawn as two columns of three holes joined by a printed rectangular loop (top bar, both side rails, bottom bar) — one net. Book I p.25: 'The lines between the terminals indicate terminals which are connected together to form a single contact.' Book V p.22 instructs 'connect four short programming wires to M10' and separately four to M11, and later 'all eight wires to M10 and M11', which requires >=4 holes each.
exceptions.citation: image_3.jpg (matrix crop); Book I p.25; Book V printed p.22

allOtherTerminals.printedCue: the two holes of one terminal sit inside a single printed oval / are joined by a short printed bar; separate terminals are separated by a gap

panelGeometry.leftBlock: six identical numbered sections, 1 at the left through 6 at the right, arranged in six horizontal bands

bands.extra: the section number 1..6 is printed above the lamp

bands.band: power strip (light-blue stripe, unlabelled except for the + and - glyphs)
bands.extra: the same blue stripe continues into the right-hand column and carries one further + and one further - (the M+ / M- pair) above the MATRIX, and ends at the word POWER

rows: row 1 (top): C (2 holes), E (2 holes), F (2 holes); a printed bracket labelled LIGHT spans C..E and a printed bracket labelled COIL spans E..F
row 2: the relay itself — round white coil on the left, contact stack on the right, plastic crossbar
row 3: the relay indicator lamp (a red lamp, one per section)
row 4: G, H, J — with N.O. printed above G, ARM above H, N.C. above J
row 5: K, L, N — with the same N.O./ARM/N.C. sense (labels printed above the row-4 holes serve both rows)
row 1: R (2 holes), S (2 holes), T (2 holes); a left-arrow is printed above R, ARM above S, a right-arrow above T
row 2: U (2 holes), V (2 holes), W (2 holes), aligned under R, S, T respectively
row 3: the red slide switch, flanked by two cream rivets (not jacks)
row 1: X (2 holes), Y (2 holes), Z (2 holes); N.O. printed above X, ARM above Y, N.C. above Z

rightColumnTopToBottom: logo plate: 'Minivac 601' with the legend 'Scientific Development Corporation, Cambridge, Massachusetts. Made in U.S.A. Patents applied for.'
continuation of the blue power stripe carrying M+ and M-, and the word POWER at the far right
MATRIX block (left) beside the POWER block (right: circuit-breaker button, ON/OFF slide switch, red power lamp above the CIRCUIT BREAKER legend). The POWER block contains NO jacks.
DECIMAL INPUT-OUTPUT block, full width of the right column

perSection.note: n = 1..6. Every entry below exists six times, once per section.

terminals.label: nA
terminals.connectsTo: one side of binary-output lamp n
terminals.citation: Book I p.6: 'The terminals labeled A and B on either side of each light are used to supply the electrical power to turn the light ON.' Panel: A printed under the left hole pair, B under the right hole pair, lamp between them.
terminals.pinnedByExperiment: Book I Experiment 2 (p.7): 1+/1A and 1-/1B lights lamp 1.

terminals.label: nB
terminals.connectsTo: the other side of binary-output lamp n
terminals.citation: Book I p.6-7; image_3.jpg

terminals.label: n+
terminals.connectsTo: the +12 V DC rail of the internal power supply (bussed to every other + terminal, including M+)
terminals.citation: Book I p.3: 'This low voltage DC is used to power MINIVAC and is connected to all terminals + and - on the power panel.'
terminals.behaviouralConfirmation: Programs throughout Books I-VI freely power a section-1 circuit from 6+ (e.g. Book I Exp.11 '6+/D16', Exp.12 '6+/5Y').

terminals.label: n-
terminals.connectsTo: the negative / return rail of the internal 12 V DC supply (bussed to every other - terminal, including M-)

terminals.connectsTo: the far side of relay-n INDICATOR LAMP; the lamp's other side lands on nE

terminals.connectsTo: the junction of relay-n indicator lamp and relay-n COIL (lamp on the C side, coil on the F side)

terminals.connectsTo: NORMALLY-OPEN fixed contact of relay-n contact set 1 (the set farther from the operator)

terminals.citation: Book I p.12; panel silkscreen 'ARM' above H

terminals.label: nJ
terminals.connectsTo: NORMALLY-CLOSED fixed contact of relay-n contact set 1

terminals.label: nK
terminals.connectsTo: NORMALLY-OPEN fixed contact of relay-n contact set 2 (the set nearer the operator)
terminals.citation: Book I p.12: 'The set of contacts closer to the operator is connected to the set of terminals closer to the operator.'

terminals.label: nL
terminals.connectsTo: the ARM of relay-n contact set 2; mechanically ganged to nH's arm by the plastic crossbar
terminals.citation: Book I p.12: 'The two arms (H & L) are connected together. Both contacts always close together.'

terminals.label: nN
terminals.connectsTo: NORMALLY-CLOSED fixed contact of relay-n contact set 2
terminals.citation: Book I p.12

terminals.label: ncom
terminals.connectsTo: nothing — a free 4-hole junction block; the four holes are common to each other only
terminals.citation: Book I p.25: 'The terminals with four holes labeled COMMON may be used when more than two connections must be made ... but are not connected to any other component.'

terminals.label: CAPACITOR (no shorthand designator is ever printed or used)

countPerSection.arithmetic: 23 two-hole terminals (A,B,+,-,C,E,F,G,H,J,K,L,N,CAPACITOR,R,S,T,U,V,W,X,Y,Z is 23 including CAPACITOR) = 46 holes, plus the 4-hole COMMON = 50

sharedRightColumn.label: M+
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the +12 V rail — same node as 1+..6+
sharedRightColumn.citation: image_3.jpg: a '+' terminal in the blue power stripe directly above the MATRIX block; Book I p.25 figure (the perspective drawing of the panel corner) shows the same '+' and '-' pair between the logo and the matrix grid; Book I p.3 states the supply 'is connected to all terminals + and - on the power panel'.
sharedRightColumn.behaviouralConfirmation: Used as a supply tap throughout: 'D16/M+' (Book IV p.? and Book V/VI, 12 occurrences), 'M+/D16' (Book I Answer 19), 'M10/M+' (Book V numeral/shape recognition), and Book V p.35 note '* Connection can be made between M+ and any point on the rotary switch dial.'

sharedRightColumn.label: M-
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the negative rail — same node as 1-..6-
sharedRightColumn.citation: image_3.jpg; Book I p.3; used as 'M-/D18' and 'D18/M-' to feed the motor RUN terminal in Book I Answers 13, 14, 15, 18 and in Book V p.22

sharedRightColumn.label: M1t..M9t
sharedRightColumn.block: MATRIX (top terminal of each of the nine tic-tac-toe cells)
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.25: 'The terminals are used as junction points, and there are no connections to the terminals below the panel.' Panel: each cell shows an upper hole-pair joined by a printed bar and a lower hole-pair joined by a printed bar, with the cell number between them.

sharedRightColumn.label: M1b..M9b
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: nothing — free junction point, electrically separate from the 't' terminal of the same cell (no printed line joins them)
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.25; image_3.jpg matrix crop; both are used independently in the Book VI tic-tac-toe program (e.g. 6H/M1t and 4H/M1b in the same listing)

sharedRightColumn.label: M10
sharedRightColumn.block: MATRIX, immediately LEFT of the 3x3 grid, at the middle row
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: nothing — a free 6-hole junction block; all six holes are one net (a printed rectangular loop joins them)
sharedRightColumn.citation: image_3.jpg crop; Book I p.25 ('lines between the terminals indicate terminals which are connected together to form a single contact'); Book V p.22 'connect four short programming wires to M10'

sharedRightColumn.label: M11
sharedRightColumn.block: MATRIX, immediately RIGHT of the 3x3 grid, at the middle row
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: nothing — a free 6-hole junction block; all six holes are one net; NOT internally joined to M10 (Book V p.22 has to add an explicit 'M10/M11' wire)
sharedRightColumn.citation: image_3.jpg crop; Book V printed p.22 program line 'M10/M11'

sharedRightColumn.label: D0 .. D15
sharedRightColumn.block: DECIMAL INPUT-OUTPUT, the ring of 16 fixed contacts around the dial
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the fixed contact for dial position N; the wiper (D16) bridges DN to D16 while the pointer points at N
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.20: 'For example, when the pointer knob points at 1, the wiper arm makes an electrical connection between D1 and D16.' image_3.jpg: dial silkscreened 0 at top then 1..15 clockwise, one two-hole pair per sector on the outer ring.
sharedRightColumn.manualErratum: Book I p.20 says the terminal number runs '(1 to 19)', but the D0 sector and its jack pair are plainly on the panel, the under-panel drawing on the same page shows a 0 contact, and D0 is wired in 13 program lines across Books IV-VI.

sharedRightColumn.label: D16 (silkscreened '16' with 'ARM' below it)
sharedRightColumn.block: DECIMAL INPUT-OUTPUT, left-hand column of jacks
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the rotary wiper arm (turns with the pointer knob)
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.20: 'The contact on the wiper arm is referred to as "D16."' and the under-panel drawing captioned 'Wiper Arm Connected to D16'; panel silkscreen '16 / ARM'.

sharedRightColumn.label: D17 (silkscreened '17'; a printed bracket labelled RUN spans 17 and 18)
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: one end of the motor-drive circuit; per the Experiment 12 schematic, D17 lands on one end of a series current-limiting RESISTOR whose other end is the D19 node
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.22: 'Power must be supplied to terminals 17 and 18 (run) to operate the motor drive.' Book I p.23 Experiment 12 circuit diagram.

sharedRightColumn.label: D18 (silkscreened '18'; RUN bracket above, STOP bracket below)
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the other end of the motor-drive circuit; per the Experiment 12 schematic, D18 lands directly on one motor terminal

sharedRightColumn.label: D19 (silkscreened '19'; a printed bracket labelled STOP spans 18 and 19)
sharedRightColumn.connectsTo: the junction between the motor and the series resistor
sharedRightColumn.citation: Book I p.22: 'A short circuit may be connected across terminals 18 and 19 (stop) to halt the motor drive.' Book I p.23 diagram; Book I p.22 'The resistors make it possible to connect a short circuit across the STOP terminals to stop the motor without over-loading the power supply.'

totals.breakdown: 6 sections x 24 terminals = 144 terminals / 300 holes; right column: M+ , M- (2), M1t..M9t + M1b..M9b (18), M10, M11 (2), D0..D19 (20) = 42 terminals; right-column holes: 4 + 36 + 12 + 40 = 92
totals.note: Arithmetic by this agent over the verified per-item counts above; the manuals never give a total.

internalBusses.citation: Book I p.3: 'This low voltage DC is used to power MINIVAC and is connected to all terminals + and - on the power panel.' All seven '+' terminals sit on the one continuous blue power stripe in image_3.jpg. Programs mix them freely.
internalBusses.caveat: The manual's sentence names 'all terminals + and -' collectively; it does not separately enumerate M+. The inclusion of M+ in the bus rests on (a) its position in the same power stripe and (b) its use as a supply tap in programs (e.g. 'D16/M+' feeding the dial, 'M-/D18' feeding the motor). No manual sentence says 'M+ is the plus rail' in so many words.

internalBusses.citation: Book I p.12: 'The two arms (H & L) are connected together. Both contacts always close together. ... The two relay arms are connected together mechanically with a plastic crossbar.' The manual's 'connected together' here is explicitly MECHANICAL (crossbar), not an electrical bus — the two contact sets are described as making 'separate electrical connections'.
Book I p.18: 'Each switch has two sets of contacts which open and close together', and the two sets make 'separate electrical connections'.
Book VI printed p.51-53 and Book III printed p.58
internalBusses.reasoning: Book I p.25 reads 'The four COMMON terminals are connected together, but are not connected to any other component.' Taken with the preceding sentence ('The terminals with four holes labeled COMMON') and the panel — which shows SIX four-hole COMMON terminals, one per section — the sentence means the four HOLES of each COMMON terminal are common to one another. It cannot mean the six COMMONs are bussed: the Book VI Secret Code program uses 1com..6com as six independent nodes ('Be sure though, that there are connections to each of the six common terminals', printed p.51) and the Electronic Maze chains them ('1com/2L', '2com/3L', '3com/4L', '4com/5L', '5com/6L', printed p.53) — a circuit that would collapse if they were bussed. Book III p.58 likewise treats 3com as a private extra contact node for light 3.

internalBusses.note: No matrix terminal is bussed to anything. Book I p.25: 'The terminals are used as junction points, and there are no connections to the terminals below the panel.' Within one terminal, the printed lines mark which holes are one contact: 2 holes for M1t..M9t and M1b..M9b, 6 holes for M10 and M11.

coil between nE and nF; the coil and the indicator lamp are in series across nC..nF

items.citation: Book I p.8-9; the break-before-make property is pinned by Experiment 3 step 8 (p.9), which has the operator find the intermediate position where both lamps are off: 'The switch breaks one connection before it makes the other connection. The pushbuttons are thus called "break-before-make" switches.'

items.topology: DPDT: arm nS selects nR (left) or nT (right); arm nV selects nU (left) or nW (right); both sets switch together
items.citation: Book I p.18; pinned by Experiment 10 (p.19), 1A/1R + 1S/1+ + 2A/1W + 1V/1S lights lamp 1 with the switch left and lamp 2 with it right

items.topology: single-pole 16-position, break-before-make: wiper D16 shorts to DN when the pointer is on N; no connection between the fixed contacts
items.citation: Book I p.20; break-before-make pinned by Experiment 11 step 3 (p.21): 'Notice that light 5 goes OFF before light 6 comes ON. ... the rotary switch is designed to disconnect the arm from one contact before making connection with the next contact.'

items.topology: Read off the Experiment 12 circuit diagram (Book I p.23): a resistor between D17 and the D19 node, and the motor between the D19 node and D18. So RUN = supply across D17/D18 (current flows D17 -> resistor -> D19 node -> motor -> D18); STOP = a short across D18/D19, which shunts the motor and leaves only the resistor across the supply.
items.tag: verified (as a reading of the diagram)
items.citation: Book I p.22 text and p.23 Experiment 12 circuit diagram
items.caveat: Book I p.22 says 'The electrical resistors used with the motor drive' (PLURAL) while the p.23 diagram shows a single zigzag. Whether there is a second resistor elsewhere in the motor branch is not settled here; the motor/rotary topic agent should check the Experiment 14 diagram (Book I p.24) and Book V motor circuits.

items.citation: Book I p.25 only says they are 'used when auxiliary components are added ... At present these terminals may be ignored.'

items.topology: isolated junction blocks, nothing behind the panel
12 V DC from a 110 V AC line transformer; a resettable circuit breaker in series; a POWER ON/OFF switch; a red power lamp. None of these four controls has a jack.
items.citation: Book I p.3 ('The power supply converts the 110-volt AC power ... to a safe working level of 12 volts DC'); image_3.jpg POWER block crop shows only the breaker button, the ON/OFF slide switch and the indicator lamp — no jacks.

experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.question: Is the relay indicator lamp a separate lamp from the binary output lamp of the same section?
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.answer: Yes. Six 'relay lights' / 'relay indicator lights' exist, one under each relay, distinct from the six BINARY OUTPUT lamps.
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.evidence: Panel photograph: a red lamp sits between the relay body and the G/H/J row in every one of the six STORAGE/PROCESSING sections. Book I p.14 drawing labels it 'Light'. Book I Experiment 7 (p.15) uses binary output lamps 1 and 2 on the relay-1 contacts AND separately lights the 'coil indicator lamp' by moving 1X/1E to 1X/1C. Books II-VI refer to 'relay light 1'..'relay light 6' as a distinct display (Book II printed p.6-7, the six-bit memory demonstration: 'Relay light 1 comes ON to indicate that a "one" is ...'; Book III printed p.58-59, relay lights 1, 2 and 3 carry the answer; Book V printed p.7-8, the speedometer reads out on the relay indicator lights).

experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.question: Which of nC / nE / nF is the lamp side and which is the bare coil side?
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.answer: nC-nE is the lamp, nE-nF is the coil.
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.evidence: Book I p.14 gives an explicit schematic (C -- LIGHT -- E -- RELAY COIL -- F) AND the behavioural test: power across C and F lights the lamp and pulls the relay; power across E and F pulls the relay with the lamp dark. The panel brackets (LIGHT over C..E, COIL over E..F) agree.

experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.question: Are the six COMMON terminals bussed to one another?
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.answer: No — they are six independent 4-hole junctions.
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.evidence: Book VI Secret Code (printed p.51): 'Be sure though, that there are connections to each of the six common terminals', and the six starred lines 2T/1com, 6W/2com, 4T/3com, 2W/4com, 6T/5com, 4W/6com each land on a different com. Electronic Maze (printed p.53) chains 1com/2L .. 5com/6L. Neither circuit works if the coms are bussed.

experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.question: Do M+ and M- exist, and are they on the power rails?
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.answer: They exist as the seventh + / - pair, in the blue power stripe above the MATRIX. Their identity as rail taps is confirmed behaviourally.
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.evidence: image_3.jpg and the Book I p.25 perspective drawing show them. Book I Answer 13-15/18 use 'M-/D18' where the same circuits elsewhere use '6-/D18' for the same purpose (compare Book I Experiment 12 p.23: '6-/D18'). Book V p.35 footnote: 'Connection can be made between M+ and any point on the rotary switch dial.'

experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.question: Does D0 exist despite the manual saying '(1 to 19)'?
experimentsThatPinDownWiringNotOtherwise.evidence: Panel dial sector '0' has its own 2-hole jack; the Book I p.20 under-panel drawing shows a contact at 0; D0 appears in 13 program lines, e.g. Book V p.22 '1J/D0', Book VI 'D15/D0', 'D10/D0', Book I Answer 18 '5Y/D0'.

notSettledBySources.question: What are the per-section CAPACITOR jacks wired to internally?
notSettledBySources.whatIsKnown: Two holes per section, in the blue COMMON/CAPACITOR stripe, immediately right of that section's COMMON. Book I p.25 says only that they are 'used when auxiliary components are added to the MINIVAC 601 in advanced programs' and 'may be ignored'. No shorthand designator for them appears anywhere in Books I-VI and no program in the six books connects to them.
notSettledBySources.whatWouldSettleIt: An under-panel photograph or the SDC service/assembly documentation for a real 601; or an SDC accessory catalogue describing the 'auxiliary components'. simulatorNotes.note: Electron-flow convention. Book I p.4 describes current as electrons flowing from the - terminal through the component to the + terminal. Polarity is irrelevant for lamps, relay coils and switch contacts, but it is load-bearing for the drive motor, whose direction reverses when the current through it reverses (Book I Experiment 14, p.24). Model the two rails as signed.

A wire plugged into either hole of a terminal reaches the same node; both holes of one terminal may be used (Book I p.4). The 4-hole COMMON and the 6-hole M10/M11 exist purely to raise the fan-out of a node.

A direct + to - wire with no component in between blows the circuit breaker (Book I p.3: 'A short circuit occurs when + is wired directly to - without a component in between'). The simulator should detect zero-impedance rail-to-rail paths and trip.

Relay contacts and pushbutton contacts are break-before-make; so is the rotary wiper. There is a real intermediate state in which neither contact is closed (Book I p.9 Exp.3 step 8; p.21 Exp.11 step 3). Circuits in the later books rely on it.

The relay indicator lamp is in SERIES with the coil across nC..nF. A consequence not demonstrated in the manuals: powering nC..nE alone would light the lamp without energising the coil. Tagged as inference, not as a manual statement.

The lamps are also the machine's current-limiting elements: Book I p.22 says the motor resistors 'limit the current which flows through the circuit in the same way that the lights limit the amount of current which flows through a relay coil'. Any electrically faithful model needs lamp resistance in the coil path.
